title: Does it work for NEW inputs?
idea: MEET. A solution must generalise. Reason about whether code that passed one example will still be right on a fresh one.

exercises.prompt: Code total = nums[0] + nums[1] printed 10 for [4, 6]. Will it work for [1, 2, 3]?
exercises.explanation: It only adds the first two items, so it ignores the third. It got lucky on a 2-item list. A real sum needs a loop.
options: No — it only adds the first two, ignoring the rest

exercises.prompt: Why re-run a passing solution with a DIFFERENT input?
exercises.explanation: One pass can be a coincidence. A fresh input checks that the logic generalises instead of fitting one example.
options: To check the logic generalises, not just fits one example
Because the first run was fake

exercises.prompt: A loop-based sum printed 10 for [2,3,5]. On [1,1,1,1] it prints...
exercises.explanation: A true accumulate adds every item: 1+1+1+1 = 4. Because it loops, it handles any length correctly.

exercises.prompt: A solution that only happens to be right for ONE input is not really solved.
exercises.explanation: Correct — it must be right for any valid input. Passing one example by luck isn't a solution, it's a coincidence.

exercises.prompt: Hardcoding total = 21 'because the example was 21' will fail when...
exercises.explanation: A hardcoded answer ignores the input entirely, so any different list gives the wrong (still 21) result.
options: The input changes to any other list

exercises.prompt: A count of '>= 50' passed on [50, 60] (got 2). A good GENERALISING re-test is...
exercises.explanation: [49, 50, 100] mixes a fail, the boundary, and a clear pass — a fresh shape that stresses the logic differently.

exercises.prompt: Order how to confirm a solution generalises.
exercises.explanation: Pick a fresh, different-shaped input, hand-work its answer, run, compare. New shape, same rigour.
blocks: Choose a new input with a different shape
Work out its answer by hand
Compare the output to the hand answer

exercises.prompt: Code passed [3,4] but fails []. What does that tell you about generalisation?
exercises.explanation: It generalises across non-empty lists but not to the empty edge. Generalisation includes the edges, not just more normal cases.
options: It doesn't yet generalise to the empty edge case

exercises.prompt: Using a loop (instead of naming fixed positions like nums[0], nums[1]) is what lets a sum generalise to any length.
exercises.explanation: Yes — a loop visits however many items there are, so the same code works for a list of 2 or 2000.

exercises.prompt: The point of this lesson is...
exercises.explanation: A solution is only proven when it's right for fresh inputs of different shapes — generalisation is the real test.
options: Confirm the solution is right for new, differently-shaped inputs
